title: The Geometric Origin of Grokking: Accelerating Generalization via Active Structural Reorganization
claim: Adding our auxiliary loss turns slow, seed-dependent, incomplete generalization into fast, consistent generalization across tasks, shown by training curves and outcome ratios.
layout: 6 panels in 2x3 grid; curves for baseline, curves for ours, then bar chart
description: A 2x3 grid of plots. The top row covers modular arithmetic and the bottom row covers tense inflection. The left column shows baseline training (solid) and validation (dashed) accuracy curves for five random seeds on a log-scale x-axis. Validation lags or stalls well below training, and the seeds diverge. The middle column shows the same curves with the R2G loss. Validation rises sharply right after training, and all seeds converge near 1.0. The right column is a bar chart of outcome ratios (Failed, Memorization, Semi-Grokking, Grokking), baseline versus R2G. In the top row, the Grokking ratio rises from 0.00 to 0.73. In the bottom row it rises from 0.00 to 0.67. Bars use light shades for the baseline and saturated shades for R2G, and the green Grokking bar stands out.
caption: The R2G loss accelerates grokking. (a-c) The modular P = 500 arithmetic task. (d-f) The tense-inflection task. Under identical
abstract: Grokking, the phenomenon where models suddenly generalize long after overfitting training data, remains a puzzling challenge in neural network dynamics. Through mechanistic analysis, we find that this transition is fundamentally driven by a structural reorganization of token representations, with the onset of grokking entailing a shift toward a well-defined geometry, and reveal the model’s distinct understanding of data’s dual characteristics. Building on these geometric insights, we propose R2G (Repel-to-Grokking) Loss, an active intervention that reshapes the representation manifold by enforcing structural repulsion. The versatility of R2G is empirically validated in both algorithmic and linguistic tasks, while our theoretical analysis and ablation studies jointly demonstrate that angular reorganization is the primary driver of grokking. Our work offers a novel mechanistic perspective on the evolution of grokking and provides a useful tool for enhancing model efficiency and reliability.
